summary: Defines a data model and a JSON representation for contact cards, for storing and exchanging address book data. It is intended as an alternative to vCard that is unambiguous, extendable, and simple to process. Unlike the earlier jCard format, it is not a direct mapping of vCard and adds meaning where appropriate.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9553 describes a way to write a contact card, such as a person's name, phone numbers and addresses, as JSON data. It is offered as a cleaner replacement for vCard, the older format for the same job, and it adds features that vCard never had. A card also names the version of the format it follows, so programs can tell whether they understand it.

questions: what is the jscontact media type
subtitle: A JSON data model for address-book cards, built as a cleaner alternative to vCard.

tldr.problem: Address books and directory services need a common way to store and exchange contact cards. The vCard format has barely changed in about ten years, and services often fall back on proprietary JSON models that no other product understands.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9553 defines a data model for contact cards and a JSON representation of it, built on I-JSON. Every part of a card is an object with named properties, and the document gives rules for validation, versioning, vendor extensions and localization.
tldr.outcome: The document registers the media type application/jscontact+json and four IANA registries for JSContact versions, properties, types and enum values, and starts at version 1.0. Two companion documents define the new vCard properties and the conversion between JSContact and vCard.

today: RFC 9553 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024, and it has not been obsoleted. It registers the media type application/jscontact+json and the initial JSContact version 1.0, and it is the first of three documents: two others define new vCard properties and the conversion between JSContact and vCard.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9553 defines a data model for contact card data and a JSON representation of that model, for storage and exchange in address book and directory applications. It aims to be an alternative to the vCard data format defined in RFC 6350, and to be unambiguous, extendable and simple to process.

The representation is built on I-JSON, a strict subset of JSON defined in RFC 7493. The document gives four design rules. The model stays mostly compatible with vCard and its extensions, adding attributes or value types where they are needed. Every attribute of a card is a simple key-value pair. The model avoids ambiguity and makes it hard to make mistakes while implementing it. And new extensions must not require a revision of the document itself.

Unlike jCard, the JSON form of vCard, JSContact is not a direct mapping of the vCard data model. It expands the semantics where the authors judged that the vCard definition was too thin or otherwise inappropriate. Two companion documents define the relation to vCard: RFC 9554 defines new vCard properties and parameters, and RFC 9555 defines how to convert between JSContact and vCard.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes how to write a contact card as JSON data. A contact card holds things like a person's name, phone numbers and addresses, and address books need a common way to store and exchange them. The format is offered as a replacement for vCard, the older text format for the same job. Two other documents cover the link to vCard: one adds new vCard properties, the other describes how to convert between the two formats.

sections.title: Objects, Properties and Type Signatures
sections.content:
Every part of a JSContact card is described as an object: a JSON object with a type name registered at IANA, one or more named properties, and a property named @type whose string value is that type name. The @type property usually does not have to be written out, because the place the object appears already implies its type. It must be set on the topmost object of the data.

Each property is declared with a type signature and a set of attributes. mandatory means the property must be present for the object to be valid. optional means it may be absent. default gives the value to use when it is omitted. defaultType names the type to assume when a property may hold more than one type.

Section 1.4 defines the data types used across the document. Id is a string of at least 1 and at most 255 characters drawn from the base64url alphabet, and it is the key type of the JSON maps that hold unordered sets of objects, so each entry in such a set has its own name. Int is a signed integer in the range -2^53+1 to 2^53-1 and UnsignedInt is an unsigned integer in the same range, both chosen so the value is exact in a floating-point double. UTCDateTime is a date-time string in the format of RFC 3339, with any letters in uppercase, the time offset written as Z, and fractional seconds only when they are non-zero and without trailing zeros, so that each moment has one representation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a card is a JSON object with named properties, and the document spells out what type each property holds and whether it has to be present. A type called Id gives every entry in a collection its own name, so a program can change one phone number without rewriting the whole card.

sections.title: Internationalization, Phonetics and Localization
sections.content:
Free-form text values, such as names and addresses, may hold any valid sequence of Unicode characters. Implementations that set bidirectional text must make sure each property value complies with the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm, and must not assume that the values of adjacent properties are processed or displayed as one string: the values of a given name component and a surname component may or may not be rendered together.

Several properties hold a URI as defined in RFC 3986. Implementations must percent-encode characters that cannot be represented using the unreserved characters of a URI.

The phonetic properties record how a value is pronounced, together with the script used and the phonetic system: ipa for the International Phonetic Alphabet, jyut for the Jyutping romanization of Cantonese, and piny for Hanyu Pinyin, the standard Mandarin romanization.

The localizations property holds the card in other languages. Its keys are language tags and its values are PatchObject values, which are sets of patches keyed by a JSON Pointer path. To localize a card, an implementation finds the language tag it wants, copies the card without the localizations property, applies the patches to the copy, and uses the copy as the localized variant. A patch may replace a whole property or a value inside it, and it must not target the localizations property itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Names and addresses can be written in any language. A card can also carry a pronunciation for a name, and a copy of the card in another language. That copy is stored as a list of changes, each one pointing at a single property to replace, so a program applies the changes it needs and leaves the rest of the card alone.

sections.title: Validation, Extensions and Versioning
sections.content:
Property names, object type names and enumerated values are case-sensitive. A property is either mandatory or optional, and in both cases its value must match the data type and definition of that property. Implementations must validate the properties registered at IANA and reject a value that breaks the definition for the version the card declares.

A property name that follows the naming rules but is unknown to an implementation must not make the card invalid. The implementation must preserve such a property, and an implementation that creates or updates a card must only set registered properties or vendor-specific ones. Preserving unknown properties is what lets two applications exchange cards without losing data when one of them knows more than the other. One property name is reserved: extra, which never names a real property, so an implementor has a safe place to put data it does not understand.

Vendors may add their own properties for experiments or for data only one service uses. A vendor-specific name starts with a prefix that is a domain name the vendor controls, followed by a colon and a name, as in example.com:foo. The prefix does not have to resolve in the Domain Name System. The prefix ietf.org and its subdomain names are reserved for IETF specifications. Implementations must preserve vendor-specific properties even when they do not know what they mean, and must not reject their values.

Every card states the JSContact version it is based on, both in the version property and in the version parameter of the media type. A major version number marks a substantial change that breaks compatibility, and implementations must be ready for property definitions that differ in a backwards-incompatible way. A minor version number marks an addition that does not break compatibility, such as a new enumerated value, and a new minor version must not require implementations to change how they process data. This document registers version 1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: A program reading a card must reject values that break the rules, and it must keep any property it does not recognise, so that data is not lost when one program knows more than another. Vendors can add their own properties under a name that starts with their domain name. Each card names the version of the format it follows, and a new major version number means the format changed in a way that older programs cannot read.

sections.title: The Card Object
sections.content:
The top-level object of JSContact data is a Card. It holds contact information, typically that of a person, an organization or a company. It carries the @type property with the value Card and the mandatory version and uid properties. The uid associates the object as the same entity across different systems, address books and views; a URN is recommended for it, a UUID in the uuid namespace is recommended, and UUID version 4 is recommended.

The kind property says what the card is about and defaults to individual. The other registered values are group, org, location, device and application. The members property lists the cards that belong to a group, keyed by their uid. The relatedTo property lists the cards related to this one, and the relation is named by a set of values such as acquaintance, agent, child, colleague, friend, neighbor, parent, sibling or spouse. An empty set means the relationship between the two objects is undefined.

Several optional properties record the history of the card. created and updated hold the times the card was created and last modified. prodId identifies the product that created it. language gives the language tag that best describes the text in the card, optionally with the script.
sections.plainLanguage: A JSContact file holds one card, and the card always carries a unique identifier and the version of the format it uses. It also records what kind of thing the card describes, such as a person or a group, and can list the other cards it is linked to. Optional properties record when the card was created and last changed, which program wrote it, and which language its text is in.

sections.title: Names, Contact Details and Resources
sections.content:
The name property holds a Name object, which is either a list of components or a full string. Each component has a mandatory kind, such as given, surname or surname2, and a mandatory value. One component value may consist of several words, so "van Gogh" is a single surname component. The isOrdered property states whether the components are in the order they should be joined in, and sortAs gives the string to compare when sorting the name by a given component type.

Contact details are held in maps whose keys are Ids. emails holds email addresses, each with an address and optional contexts, pref and label. phones holds numbers, each with a number that may be a URI such as a tel URI, and a features set naming what the number supports, such as mobile, voice, text, video, main-number, textphone, fax or pager. onlineServices holds messaging and social media accounts, and preferredLanguages holds the languages to use when writing to the person.

The pref property orders contact details of the same type. Its value must be between 1 and 100, lower values mean a higher preference, and detail with no preference is treated as least preferred. The contexts property marks whether a detail is for private or work use, and label holds a short custom label for it.

Resources are described by a Resource type with a mandatory uri and optional kind, mediaType, contexts, pref and label. The cryptoKeys, directories, links and media properties use it: media distinguishes a photo, a sound and a logo, and a links entry of kind contact gives a way to reach the person. The addresses property holds postal addresses and locations, each made of components or given as a full string, a country code, coordinates or a time zone. Finally keywords, notes, anniversaries and personalInfo hold the remaining free-text extras.
sections.plainLanguage: A card lists a person's name either as ordered pieces, such as a given name and a surname, or as one string. Phone numbers, email addresses and online accounts each sit in a list, and each one can say whether it is for home or work and which to try first. That order runs from 1 to 100, where 1 is tried first. Addresses, photographs, keys and links are stored the same way, each one pointing at a URI.

sections.title: Media Type and IANA Registries
sections.content:
The document registers the media type application/jscontact+json for JSContact data in JSON. It has one optional parameter, version, which conveys the version of the data in the body part and must not occur more than once; when it is present, the values of all version properties in the body part must match it. The encoding considerations are those of application/json in RFC 8259, and a JSON Pointer may be used as a fragment identifier.

IANA has created a JSContact registry group with four registries: JSContact Version, JSContact Properties, JSContact Types and JSContact Enum Values. The version registry defines the allowed range of major and minor version numbers, and its first entry is major version 1 with a highest minor version of 0.

A registration follows an administrative procedure rather than a formal standards process. Notice of a proposed registration goes to the Calext working group mailing list, then to IANA, then to a designated expert, whose main concerns are preventing name collisions and making sure the submitter has documented the security and privacy considerations. Every registration carries an intended usage of common, reserved or obsolete, and the designated expert decides whether the change needs a new major or minor version. A change that is backwards-incompatible follows the Standards Action policy; other changes follow Specification Required. Registered items are never deleted: an item no longer considered appropriate is declared obsolete by changing its intended usage.
sections.plainLanguage: Files in this format are sent with the media type application/jscontact+json, and that type carries an optional parameter naming the version of the data. Four registries at IANA hold the version numbers, the property names, the type names and the allowed values. Anyone can propose a new entry: the request goes to the working group, then to IANA, then to an expert who checks that the name does not clash with an existing one and that the proposer explained the security and privacy effects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Contact information is very privacy sensitive. It can reveal a person's identity, location, credentials, employment status, interests and social network, so its transmission and storage must be done carefully to protect it from eavesdropping, replay, message insertion, deletion, modification and on-path attacks. The document only defines the data format, so these safeguards are mainly the concern of the API or method used to store and transmit the files.

For JSON parsing, the security considerations of RFC 8259 apply. Parsers must check the syntax of the supplied data thoroughly. A scan for a matching closing bracket can run into the end of the supplied data, which is an error condition, and escape sequences must be fully formed before the special processing they trigger is applied, with care when they sit next to other special characters or next to the end of the data. Because JSON strings carry no explicit length, the risk of resource exhaustion is small, but implementations may still want to limit the size of the allocations they accept from untrusted data.

URI values need extra care. Connections to remote resources should use well-known ports and allowed protocols, generally just HTTP and HTTPS on their default ports, and the URL should be resolved so that it cannot reach internal resources. Connecting to an external source reveals the IP address and therefore often the location of the user. A maliciously constructed card may hold a very large number of URIs, and in a published address book with many subscribers such a card could be widely distributed, so implementations should limit the automatic fetching of linked resources to reduce the risk of a denial-of-service amplification.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact card can reveal a lot about a person, so the document warns that the way the data is stored and sent matters as much as the format itself. Two risks stand out. A parser must stop at the end of the data instead of scanning for a closing bracket that is not there. And a card can carry a very long list of links, so a program should fetch only some of them automatically, because making every recipient of a published address book fetch the same link at once turns that card into a way to attack them all.
